growth_story.headline: Income per person in the U.S. Virgin Islands was 26.3 percent below its 2008 peak in 2022, after a refinery closed and hurricanes hit; tourism has recovered.
growth_story.arc: From 2003 to 2010 income per person grew 1.2 percent a year, with gains of 3.3 to 4.0 percent a year in 2004–2007, before it peaked in 2008 and fell 6.6 percent in 2009 in the financial recession. From 2011 to 2022 it shrank by 1.9 percent a year, with the deepest falls in 2011 and 2012 (8.1 and 14.7 percent), as the Hovensa oil refinery on St. Croix closed over 2012 and 2013. After hurricanes Irma and Maria in 2017, federal disaster aid, tourism and building work for a refinery restart lifted growth to 2.1 percent in 2018 and 3.2 percent in 2019, until the COVID-19 pandemic cut the recovery short in 2020. Over 2016–2022 growth averaged 1.2 percent a year, close to the 1.4 percent typical of similar economies, but in 2022 income per person was still 26.3 percent below the 2008 peak and lower than in 2002. The record stops in 2022 because the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis suspended its GDP estimates for the territory.

threads.title: The refinery closes
threads.text: The territory's government counts the closure of the Hovensa oil refinery over 2012 and 2013 among three major shocks, alongside the 2008 recession and the 2017 hurricanes. Income per person fell 14.7 percent in 2012 and 6.2 percent in 2013.

threads.title: Hurricanes, aid and the pandemic
threads.text: After the 2017 hurricanes, a recovery came, driven mostly by federal disaster aid, tourism spending and building work for a refinery restart. The COVID-19 pandemic ended it in March 2020. Federal relief payments then held up household spending, and income per person grew 4.1 percent in 2021.

The refinery itself has not restarted, and no GDP figures have been published since the 2022 estimates.

growth_story.tension: The territory's finance department told the legislature in 2024 that output had grown steadily since the refinery closed, matching pre-closure levels in 2022, and had returned to a growth trend since 2019. The data tell a different story for income per person: in 2022 it was still 26.3 percent below the 2008 peak, and it fell in 2020 and again in 2022. The sources speak of total output, while the data measure income per person, and the record cannot show how much of the gap comes from changes in population.
